 How this election works Content closed. Americans are electing members of Congress, which is made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 House seats are up for election. In the Senate, only 35 of 100 seats are being contested because senators serve six-year terms. This results tracker shows both the races being decided now and the 65 seats that are not up for election this year - 34 held by Democrats and 31 by Republicans.
 Live .  38,537 viewing 38537 viewing Live page Updated 3 minutes ago Top Democrat says Congress will rein in 'out-of-control' Trump administration after midterms win
 Summary
 A top Democrat says Congress will rein in "an out-of-control executive branch" after his party won control of both houses in the midterm elections
 Hakeem Jeffries - likely to be the next Speaker of the House - accuses the "Trump Cartel" of "massive corruption" and adds: "We are going to hold the crooks accountable"
 After the Democrats' resounding win in Tuesday's elections, President Trump said it was "largely true" the Iran war was to blame for the Republican Party's defeat
 That followed comments from Vice-President JD Vance, who said "everyone knows" the war was why his party lost
 Analysis: Is Vance trying to distance himself from Trump before running for president himself? 
 Meanwhile, oil prices have fallen to their lowest level in two months in the wake of the result

 next page Midterms through the lens of war: Reaction in Ukraine, Russia and Iran published at 17:30 GMT 4 November 17:30 GMT 4 November 
 BBC Monitoring 
 Image source, Tehran Times Image caption, The Tehran Times pokes fund at Trump with a play on "Midnight Hammer" - the name of the operation that saw the US bomb Iranian nuclear sites last year
 For people in Ukraine, Iran and across the Middle East, the US midterms were less about domestic politics and more about what the result could mean for ongoing conflicts.
 In Ukraine, commentators focused on Trump's handling of the war, with journalist Roman Tsymbalyuk quipping the president had "settled every war but lost his own" - a reference to Trump's repeated claims about ending global conflicts. 
 As Russia continues to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure, some in Kyiv hope Democratic gains could strengthen support for tougher sanctions on Moscow, while others fear political gridlock in Washington could create fresh uncertainty over Ukraine policy.
 In Moscow, the Kremlin publicly expressed hope that Trump would continue efforts to broker an end to the war, with further Russia-Ukraine talks expected this month. But pro-war Russian voices warned that a Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain Trump's ability to deliver any future agreements with the Kremlin or ease sanctions on Russia.
 Meanwhile, Iran's leadership and state-linked media portrayed Democratic gains as a public rebuke of Trump's war policy. Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf argued that Americans had "said no to war", while Iranian media highlighted what they described as the growing political cost of military confrontation with Tehran.

 Can Trump use his veto to block Democrat laws? published at 17:24 GMT 4 November 17:24 GMT 4 November 
 By Tom Edgington 
 President Donald Trump posted an image of a red baseball cap bearing the word "VETO" following the Democrats' midterm election victory overnight.
 He told Fox News that he could send legislation back to Congress "with a nice stamp 'veto' and there's not a thing they can do about that".
 It's true presidents have a constitutional power to reject planned laws passed by Congress, but this power isn't absolute. 
 Under the US Constitution, Congress can normally override vetoes if two-thirds of the House and Senate vote to do so - but the Democrats are short of that and would need Republican support.
 That said, one of Trump’s vetoes - over defence spending - was successfully overturned in 2021 . But this is rare. 
 According to Congress, only about 4% of all vetoes have been successfully overturned.
 Trump could also continue to use executive orders, which don't require congressional approval.
 US politics expert Clodagh Harrington, from University College Cork, tells BBC Verify that Congress doesn't have much sway to override executive orders. 
 "But they can be challenged in court and that's the more textbook way to prevent them."

 'I'm very confident that we're going to win,' says Mississippi Democratic candidate published at 17:08 GMT 4 November 17:08 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Colom pictured at a campaign rally at the end of last month
 Scott Colom, the Democratic candidate for Mississippi's Senate seat, says he is "very happy" about where the race currently stands.
 He tells a news conference: "I'm very confident about where we are and I'm very confident that we're going to win."
 At 10:00 ET (15:00 GMT), only 43 votes separated Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for the seat, with 96% of the vote counted, according to AP.
 Colom says that those who voted by affidavit ballots - also known as provisional ballots - due to problems such as not having voter ID available will have until 10 November to resolve any issues.
 The Democrat's campaign earlier estimated there are 15,000 affidavit ballots that remain to be counted, the BBC's US partner CBS News reports.
 The candidate says he does not want to estimate the time it will take for the count to be completed, but wishes to ensure the process is protected.
 "We have got lawyers who are ready to make sure that the law is followed," he adds.

 Midterms 'close to an extinction-level event' for Republicans, says DeSantis published at 17:03 GMT 4 November 17:03 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, AP Florida Governor Ron DeSantis says the Republicans have suffered "close to an extinction-level event" following their losses in the midterm elections. 
 Speaking during a news conference, the outgoing Republican governor says the results will have a "huge" impact and are "probably the political worst case scenario for a midterm election".
 He says that keeping the US Senate "would have been a win", even if his party lost two or three seats.
 "We knew it could be worse, but I don't think most of us thought it would be quite this bad," he says.
 DeSantis adds the party is "in a deep hole nationally because of this election", but emphasises "this was a rejection of Republicans in Washington" and not voters taking a "positive view" of the Democrats.

 Tackling rising costs and 'rampant' corruption are top priorities - Schumer published at 16:58 GMT 4 November 16:58 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, EPA/Shutterstock The US Senate has undergone a "generational remake" that will have "huge consequences for history", the top Democrat in the chamber, Chuck Schumer, says. 
 Schumer, currently the minority leader in the Senate, says voters told Democrats that they wanted the party to address two primary issues: the cost of living and corruption in government. 
 "We have an amazing crop of new senators," Schumer says at a press conference in Washington. "What we have now seen is a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America." 
 Schumer says Democrats are also willing to launch investigations into US President Donald Trump. 
 "Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire," he says. 
 "The days of Trump's supplicant Senate are over."
 Asked how far the Democrats will go with investigations, Schumer says they need to take place because "there was such rampant corruption". 
 "But we're not going to take our eye of the ball," he says. "Number one: Reducing costs, ending corruption."

 'Republican loss caused by Iran and economy' - what Vance has said published at 16:51 GMT 4 November 16:51 GMT 4 November 
 Grace Eliza Goodwin 
US reporter 
 As we've been reporting, Vice-President JD Vance has shared a lengthy post on social media that gives his take on the Republican defeat in elections.
 Here are some key points he made: 
 The main problem, Vance says, was not that Republicans didn't turn out to vote - it was that "many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026 "
 That's partly because "our economic messaging wasn't sharp enough "
 But what those former Trump voters cared most about was for Republicans to end the war in Iran, focus on inflation and the cost of living, put America first, and change the US relationship to Israel, Vance says, pointing to recent polling
 He also says he's open to the idea of changing immigration enforcement by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour
 The real reason Republicans lost is the war in Iran, he says, adding that Trump agrees
 To those who are upset about the results of the midterms, Vance says: "Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

 Vance offers blunt post-mortem on election results published at 16:19 GMT 4 November 16:19 GMT 4 November 
 Daniel Bush 
Washington correspondent 
 JD Vance believes the Iran war cost Republicans control of Congress. The vice-president says "the reason we lost is the war", in a lengthy election post-mortem statement that offers an unusually candid assessment of the midterm elections.
 Vance acknowledges that the Iran war, rising costs and other issues led Republican voters who backed him and President Donald Trump in 2024 to abandon the party this year.
 He also notes that voters took issue with the administration’s immigration agenda, and says he was open to some reforms.
 Vance notes that Trump also singled out frustration over the war with Iran last night. Still, the US vice-president was more blunt than Trump after months of backing the war in public.
 The statement immediately fuelled interest in Vance’s 2028 plans, as pundits speculate that he used the moment to signal his plans to run for the White House.
 Vance has sidestepped that question up until now. But with the midterms in the rear-view mirror, he’ll face growing pressure to announce a decision soon.

 'The reason we lost is the war,' JD Vance says published at 15:53 GMT 4 November 15:53 GMT 4 November Breaking 
 US Vice-President JD Vance reacts to Republicans' midterm loss in a lengthy post on X, claiming the US war in Iran was the reason for his party's defeat.
 "The reason we lost is the war," he says.
 "Everyone knows why we lost," he goes on to say. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Vance campaigned on Tuesday in Ohio

 It may take weeks to learn who won the Alaska Senate race published at 15:51 GMT 4 November 15:51 GMT 4 November 
 Grace Eliza Goodwin 
US reporter 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images It may be weeks before we know the results of Alaska's Senate race - one of the most competitive in the country.
 There, incumbent Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan is running against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola and, in a twist that has stirred controversy , against an independent candidate named Daniel J Sullivan.
 The expected delay is partly because Alaska has ranked-choice ballots, where voters can select more than one candidate in order of preference. And if a single candidate doesn't win a clear majority then the state recounts the ballots in a second round with the last-place candidate removed. 
 On top of that, Alaska allows 10 to 15 days for mailed ballots to be returned to the elections office.
 "The results are not going to be fast, but Alaskans are patient," Peltola told supporters on election night.

 When will we know the results of the Mississippi election? published at 15:49 GMT 4 November 15:49 GMT 4 November 
 It could take a while.
 Democratic candidate Scott Colom is challenging Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for Mississippi's Senate seat.
 At 10:00 ET (15:00 GMT), 43 votes separated the two candidates, with 96% of the vote counted, according to AP. The race is still too close to call.
 While we may have a result today, it could also take several days for all the votes to be counted.

 Republicans will 'double down' following losses, says House Speaker published at 15:40 GMT 4 November 15:40 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, Reuters Addressing supporters in Louisiana last night, Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives Mike Johnson said: "Republicans will not be deterred by the outcome of one election. In fact, you know what we do? We double down." 
 He added that in the 2028 election Republicans would "take back the House and we will finish this job".
 While Johnson, 54, won his race to return to the House, this morning he has said he will not run for House minority leader - which will become the top Republican post in the chamber once Democrats take control in January - according to reports.
 Johnson has spent three years in the role, having replaced former Speaker Kevin McCarthy in October 2023 after a contentious selection process within the Republican party.
 He began his career as a constitutional lawyer, spending close to 20 years in the profession before entering politics.

 Republican strategist says party needs to 'adjust to reality' after Democrats' sweep published at 15:28 GMT 4 November 15:28 GMT 4 November 
 Grace Eliza Goodwin 
US reporter 
 What do Republicans think of last night's Democratic victory? I asked one of the party's strategists.
 Mark Bednar, who worked on the Trump-Vance transition team after the presidential election, tells the BBC it's clear his party "did not excite the Trump coalition that won a historic victory in 2024".
 He says we can expect that with control of Congress, Democrats will use a lot of their energy to investigate - and possibly try to impeach - President Trump. 
 "But they will have their own internal fights that will only grow," Bednar adds. 
 And, he warns: "Republicans need to adjust to the reality that President Trump alone cannot be the driving force for voter turnout."

 Speaker Mike Johnson will not run for House minority leader published at 15:11 GMT 4 November 15:11 GMT 4 November Breaking 
 Image source, Getty Images In an all-staff call this morning, Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives Mike Johnson has confirmed he won't run for the minority leader position when Democrats take control of Congress in January, US media reports.
 He added that he spoke with President Trump earlier this morning. 
 Addressing supporters in Louisiana last night, Johnson had said he was "disappointed" by the election's results.

 Big swings for tech giants after midterms - but not all were winners published at 15:03 GMT 4 November 15:03 GMT 4 November 
 Mitchell Labiak 
Business reporter 
 US tech giants' share prices jumped on opening the morning after Democrats took both chambers of Congress, with Amazon, Microsoft, and Apple leaping 7.5%, 5.5%, and 5% respectively.
 As a general rule investors like certainty, which is what a Democrat-controlled Congress could give US politics for the next two years.
 But not all tech giants were winners. 
 Elon Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX were down 4.9% and 3.4%, after many Democrats came out in opposition to the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres on the campaign trail.
 Musk's relationship with Democrats could also be a factor. He spent millions in political donations against them in the midterms and he has been a vocal – and often controversial – critic of theirs for years.
 As such, some investors might be considering what the erratic businessman's relationship with politics could mean for his companies when Democrats have so much control.

 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for defeat published at 14:53 GMT 4 November 14:53 GMT 4 November 
 Daniel Bush 
Washington correspondent 
 Image source, Getty Images "It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Republican lobbyist Bill Miller tells me, shortly after the midterm results became clear. 
 "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this," he adds.
 Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night has quickly given way to anger with US president .
 After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.
 "It was just one mistake after another," says Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota, adding: "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
 A White House ally of Trump said anger with the president "is extremely high" after the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm".

 US markets up in early trading published at 14:48 GMT 4 November 14:48 GMT 4 November 
 Mitchell Labiak 
Business reporter 
 The S&P 500 index of the largest firms listed in the US opened up 1.13% following a series of historic wins for Democrats in the midterm elections.
 Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index was up 1.17% on opening while the Dow Jones index was up 2.3%

 Talarico denounces big money in politics and slams Musk published at 14:37 GMT 4 November 14:37 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images James Talarico, the Democrat who has flipped a crucial Texas Senate seat from Republicans, says one of his biggest priorities in Congress will be to "get big money out of our politics". 
 "Last night the people of Texas delivered a crystal clear message to the world's first trillionaire," he tells CBS, referencing Elon Musk, who poured more than $47m (£35m) into the campaign of Talarico's opponent, Republican Ken Paxton. "Texas is not for sale."
 "We're all tired of these billionaires who own the algorithms, who own so many of the news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens," he adds.

 Democrats need to tackle affordability and Trump must end war - Jeffries published at 14:28 GMT 4 November 14:28 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Now that Democrats have won a majority in the House of Representatives, Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, formerly the House Minority Leader, is poised to become the first black Speaker of the House. 
 Last night's blue wave was "an incredible victory for the American people all across the country, and a stunning rebuke [of] MAGA extremism", Jeffries tells MS Now's Joe Scarborough.
 Responding to a question on what comes next for his party, Jeffries says "we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability".
 Turning to Congress, Scarborough asks about Trump's priorities for lawmakers.
 Jeffries says the president needs to end the war in Iran, before the new Congress even takes power in January. 
 "That was clearly one of the messages that the American people decisively sent last evening," he says.

 Dozens of House seats yet to be declared as Democrats take majority published at 14:19 GMT 4 November 14:19 GMT 4 November 
 In the US House of Representatives, where all of its 435 seats were up for grabs in this election, there are still 68 that are yet to be confirmed. 
 The Democrats have so far won 228 seats, already comfortably past the 218 required for a majority, and have flipped 25 of those from the Republicans. 
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 'Trump is still your president', White House writes on social media published at 14:11 GMT 4 November 14:11 GMT 4 November 
 Image source, The White House/X We're seeing the first remarks this morning from the White House in the wake of the Democrats' significant gains.
 The official account for the White House posts an image of Trump leaning over the Resolute Desk, with a "public service announcement". Imposed on the image are the words: "PSA: Trump is still your president".
 Trump reacted to the Republican defeat earlier today, conceding that Democrats "did a good job", while claiming Republican candidates would have done better had he been on the ballot.
